Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Amara was twenty-one, but she felt ancient. The six months since her honorable discharge had hollowed her out, leaving a brittle shell where a confident soldier and, before that, a vibrant young woman, had once been. She had taken a job as a peer counselor at a local veterans’ outreach center, thinking that helping others navigate their return to civilian life might help her find her own way back. Instead, the role had become a stage for her own unraveling. The precipitating event was a night mission she now referred to only as “the extraction.” Her unit was tasked with evacuating a wounded soldier from a contested village under the cover of night. The darkness was absolute, a thick, suffocating blanket broken only by the dim red light inside their vehicle. As the helicopter descended, its percussive thumping seemed to shake the very air from her lungs. Her squad mate, a young man who talked endlessly of his wife and two small daughters, leaned over and shouted above the rotor wash, “Almost home to the family.” In that instant, the world erupted in fire and chaos.

Now, any similar sound sends her right back to the dust and confusion of that landing zone. Last week, while in a session with a client, the distant thrum of a traffic helicopter passing overhead caused her to freeze mid-sentence. The sterile quiet of her office was suddenly filled with the scent of jet fuel and hot metal, and she had to grip the arms of her chair to keep from diving under the desk. She has also come to fear the dark, a primal terror she had never known, even in the field. She sleeps with a hallway light on and a lamp by her bed, and the walk to her car through the dimly lit parking garage after her evening shifts is a nightly trial. Every shadow seems to hold a threat, every flicker of movement a potential ambush.

The deepest cuts, however, are reserved for any mention of family. When a client speaks of their children, or a colleague complains about a call from their mother, the memory of her squad mate’s final words slices through her. She sees his face, hears his voice over the rotors, and is flooded with a guilt so profound it feels like drowning. She has come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with her, some intrinsic flaw in her judgment that led to the disaster. She replays the moments before the attack endlessly, convinced that a different position, a faster command, any small change on her part would have altered the outcome. Somebody else, a better soldier, she is certain, would not have gotten into that situation; they would have saved him.

This conviction has poisoned her life from the inside out. The woman who once led a team now feels incapable of managing even the simplest social interactions. She has systematically cut herself off from the people who knew her before. Texts from her old army buddies go unanswered; their invitations to meet up are met with silence. She tells herself they wouldn’t understand the person she has become, but the deeper truth is that she cannot bear for them to see her. The idea of forming new connections is even more daunting. At work, she maintains a professional but impenetrable distance, deflecting personal questions and turning down invitations for coffee. She avoids the news and can no longer watch movies, especially not the action films she used to love. The risk of encountering a scene of combat, of hearing the familiar sounds or seeing the familiar chaos, is too great.

Her isolation became unsustainable. A few weeks ago, a veteran she was counseling spoke emotionally about his guilt over missing his daughter’s birthday during his last tour. Amara felt a familiar cold dread creep up her spine. She saw her squad mate’s face, not the client’s. She abruptly ended the session, claiming a sudden migraine, and fled to the bathroom, where she choked back sobs. The incident led to a gentle but firm conversation with her supervisor. It was that conversation, the fear of losing the one remaining piece of her identity—the helper, the counselor—that finally propelled her to seek help. She is terrified of what this process will unearth, but the alternative, a life lived in the shadows, has become even more frightening.
